docs.title: Controls Crash Course
docs.text:
An interactive control theory crash course for software engineers. It starts with classical time- and frequency-domain analysis and works up to whole-body control of a 7-DOF robot arm.

Each chapter pairs a short explanation with interactive widgets that run right in the page. Change a parameter, watch the system respond, and build intuition before the math gets heavy.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
1. Time Domain: dynamic systems, state space and linearization, and discrete time.
  2. Frequency Domain (coming soon): the Laplace transform, transfer functions, poles and zeros, and Bode plots.
  3. Feedback and Joint Control (coming soon): PID control, root locus, and stability margins.
  4. Kinematics (coming soon): rotations and transforms, forward kinematics, the Jacobian, singularities, inverse kinematics, and redundancy.
  5. Rigid-Body Dynamics (coming soon): the manipulator equations, Pinocchio's algorithms, and computed-torque control.
  6. Task-Space Control (coming soon): operational-space control, null-space projection, and impedance control.
  7. Whole-Body Control (coming soon): quadratic programming and task-space inverse dynamics on a 7-DOF arm.

docs.title: Discrete Time
docs.text: Computers work in steps. A simulator advances the state by a time step \(\Delta t\) at a time, and a controller reads its sensors and updates its command once per cycle. Replacing smooth time with steps can go wrong.

docs.title: Forward Euler
docs.text:
The simplest method assumes the derivative stays constant over one step:

\[ \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \Delta t\, f(\mathbf{x}_k, u_k) \]

This is the line inside the loop of the Eigen example on the previous page.

docs.title: When it blows up
docs.text:
Apply it to the cart with no push, \(\dot{v} = -v/\tau\). Each step multiplies the speed by \(1 - \Delta t/\tau\):

  • \(\Delta t < \tau\): the speed decays, as it should.
  • \(\tau < \Delta t < 2\tau\): the speed flips sign every step, an oscillation the real cart can't do.
  • \(\Delta t > 2\tau\): the speed grows without bound. The simulation is numerically unstable.

Oscillators are worse. For an undamped spring, forward Euler adds a little energy every step, so the oscillation grows no matter how small \(\Delta t\) is.

Rule of thumb

Keep the time step small compared to the system's fastest time scale: its smallest \(\tau\) or \(1/\omega_n\).

docs.title: Better integrators
docs.text: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) evaluates the derivative four times per step and is far more accurate and stable. The mass-spring-damper widget uses it with a 1 ms step. Chapter 3 covers the controller side: how a loop's update rate limits its feedback.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Franklin, Powell, and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems. It writes state space as \(F, G, H, J\) where we use \(A, B, C, D\).
  • Spong, Hutchinson, and Vidyasagar, Robot Modeling and Control, whose notation this course follows.

Lab: time_domain (coming soon)

The C++ lab simulates the mass-spring-damper open loop and logs its step and impulse responses to Rerun.

docs.title: State Space and Linearization
docs.text: A robot arm has dozens of coupled equations of motion, so we need one uniform form that a computer can handle. State space is that form, and it turns calculus into linear algebra.

docs.title: From one equation to many
docs.text:
Give every derivative except the highest its own name. For the mass-spring-damper, let \(x_1 = x\) (position) and \(x_2 = \dot{x}\) (velocity). The second-order equation becomes two first-order ones:

\[ \dot{x}_1 = x_2, \qquad \dot{x}_2 = -\frac{k}{m}x_1 - \frac{b}{m}x_2 + \frac{1}{m}u \]

An \(N\)th-order equation always becomes \(N\) first-order equations this way.

docs.title: The matrix form
docs.text:
Stack the states into a vector \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1,\ x_2]^T\) (bold, to tell it apart from the displacement \(x\)):

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} + Bu, \qquad y = C\mathbf{x} + Du \] \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -k/m & -b/m \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1/m \end{bmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = 0 \]
  • \(A\) holds the system's own dynamics. Its frequencies and damping live here.
  • \(B\) says how the input pushes the state.
  • \(C\) picks out the measured output, here the position. \(D\) is a direct path from input to output, usually zero.

A 7-joint robot arm needs bigger matrices, but the equation keeps the same shape. In C++ with Eigen:

#include <Eigen/Dense>

const double m = 1.0, b = 1.0, k = 10.0;
Eigen::Matrix2d A;
A << 0.0,    1.0,
     -k / m, -b / m;
const Eigen::Vector2d B(0.0, 1.0 / m);

Eigen::Vector2d x(1.0, 0.0);  // state: [position, velocity]
const double dt = 0.001, u = 0.0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) {
  x += dt * (A * x + B * u);  // one forward Euler step (see Discrete Time)
}

docs.title: Linearization
docs.text:
Real systems are nonlinear: \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}, u)\). But near an equilibrium, a state where \(f = 0\) and nothing changes, they behave almost linearly. The \(A\) matrix is then \(\partial f / \partial \mathbf{x}\) evaluated at the equilibrium, a matrix of partial derivatives called a Jacobian.

A pendulum of length \(l\) with mass \(m\) at its tip, pivot friction \(b\), and motor torque \(\tau\) follows

\[ ml^2\ddot{\theta} + b\dot{\theta} + mgl\sin\theta = \tau \]

Linearizing around an angle \(\bar{\theta}\) gives

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\dfrac{g}{l}\cos\bar{\theta} & -\dfrac{b}{ml^2} \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Hanging down (\(\bar{\theta} = 0\)): the bottom-left entry is \(-g/l\), just like the spring's \(-k/m\). Gravity acts as a spring.
  • Balanced upright (\(\bar{\theta} = \pi\)): it flips to \(+g/l\), a "negative spring" that pushes the pendulum away. It falls. Chapter 2 shows how to test for this.

The approximation only holds near the equilibrium, which is why controllers built on it work best when they keep the system close to its operating point.

docs.title: Dynamic Systems
docs.text: A dynamic system is one whose output depends on its history, not just its current input. Push a cart and let go: it keeps rolling. We describe these systems with differential equations, in terms of an input \(u\) we act on (a force, a torque), an output \(y\) we measure, and a state: the smallest set of variables that, together with future inputs, determines the future. If you'd need to save it to pause and resume a simulation, it's state.

docs.title: First-order systems
docs.text:
A cart of mass \(m\) is pushed with force \(u\) against viscous drag \(-bv\):

\[ m\dot{v} + bv = u \]

Push with a constant force and the speed rises toward \(u/b\) along an exponential curve with time constant \(\tau = m/b\). It reaches 63% of its final speed after \(\tau\) seconds and is essentially done after \(4\tau\).

docs.title: Second-order systems
docs.text:
Add a spring and the system can store energy in two places, as motion and as spring stretch, and trade it back and forth. That's what makes oscillation possible.

A block of mass \(m\) is connected to a wall by a spring of stiffness \(k\) and a damper with coefficient \(b\). With displacement \(x\) from rest and an applied force \(u\), Newton's second law gives

\[ m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = u \]

Two numbers summarize its behavior:

\[ \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{km}} \]

The natural frequency \(\omega_n\) (rad/s) sets how fast it wants to oscillate. The damping ratio \(\zeta\) decides how the motion dies out:

Damping ratio Behavior \(\zeta = 0\) Undamped: oscillates forever. \(0 < \zeta < 1\) Underdamped: oscillates with a decaying envelope. \(\zeta = 1\) Critically damped: fastest return to rest without overshooting. \(\zeta > 1\) Overdamped: creeps back to rest without oscillating.

A robot joint under feedback control behaves much like this system, so it's worth building a feel for it.

docs.title: Impulse response
docs.text:
An impulse is a sharp strike, like a hammer tap. It changes the block's velocity instantly by \(\Delta v = J/m\), where \(J\) is the impulse. The block then rings at its natural frequency inside an envelope that decays at a rate set by \(\zeta\).

The impulse response formula

Starting from rest, an underdamped block struck with impulse \(J\) moves as

\[ x(t) = \frac{J}{m\,\omega_d}\, e^{-\zeta\omega_n t} \sin(\omega_d t), \qquad \omega_d = \omega_n\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2} \]

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
The block has mass \(m = 1\text{ kg}\), and each press of Impulse adds \(1.5\) m/s to its velocity. Change \(k\) and \(b\) at any time, even mid-swing.

  • Set \(b = 0\). It oscillates forever.
  • For \(k = 10\) N/m, find the \(b\) that gives critical damping.
  • With \(b = 0\), press Impulse in time with the swing. That's resonance.
Spring constant k = N/m Damping coefficient b = N·s/m Impulse
